title: The Ninth Harvest Moon
subtitle: The Legend of Toma
teaser: Lord Itagaki burned the Kurosawa valley at harvest and chained the village gate from outside. For nine years after, at every harvest moon, one more of his men heard the rice whisper in the dark.

sections.heading: I. The Sound in the Rice
paragraphs: In the Kurosawa valley, when the rice was ripe and the wind came down off the hills, the fields made a sound like someone hushing a child.
Shhh.

The farmers said it was the rice god telling the valley to be quiet, so it could hear the grain swell. On the first day of harvest, every family tied a red ribbon around the first sheaf they cut, in a knot used for nothing else, and hung it over the door. That was the god’s share. The rest was theirs.

Toma farmed four terraces on the east slope. He had a wife, two sons, an old mother, and a reaping sickle he had sharpened so often that the blade was as thin as a new moon. Nobody in the valley thought about him much. That suited him.

In the ninth month, Lord Hamura’s army came over the hills, hungry. Lord Itagaki Munetaka, who held the valley, did not want to fight it. He did the arithmetic instead. An army that cannot eat cannot march.
He ordered the valley burned.

Eight of his soldiers went to Kurosawa with torches and pitch. The village had a stockade and one gate, and they did not wait for it to empty. They swung the gate shut, dropped the oak bar across it from outside, and wound an iron chain round and round the bar and the posts. Then they lit the fields.
The rice was dry and ready. It went up like paper.
Two hundred and twelve people died inside that stockade. Toma’s mother died there, and his wife, and both his sons. There is nothing more to say about that.
Toma died last. He died at the gate with his arm through a gap in the planks, hacking at the bar with his reaping sickle. When the fire reached him he was two thirds of the way through the oak.
On the other side, the eight soldiers listened to the blade biting wood until it stopped. Then they went home.

sections.heading: II. What Stood Up in the Ash
paragraphs: A month later the harvest moon rose over the black fields of Kurosawa, and a charcoal burner on the ridge saw something stand up out of the ash.

It was tall and very thin. It wore a long white robe, the kind the dead are dressed in for burial, though nobody had dressed the dead of Kurosawa. Its black hair hung past its waist, with red ribbons knotted through it. When it walked, it dragged an iron chain behind it through the ash, and on the end of the chain was a sickle.
It went to the gate first and stood there for a long time. Then it turned toward the castle town. The charcoal burner lay flat in the ferns until morning, and never went up that ridge again.
Gonroku, the soldier who had wound the chain, was asleep in the barracks with nineteen other men. He woke in the dark because he heard the rice.
Shhh.

There was no rice within a mile of the barracks. It was the sound of a ripe field in the wind, coming closer, stalk by stalk. The lamp by the door had burned down to a blue bead. As he watched, it turned green.
Something white was standing at the foot of his bed.

Nineteen men slept through it. In the morning they found Gonroku in his blankets with his hair gone white. His skin was grey and creased like old paper, and when they lifted him he weighed no more than a sheaf of straw. Around his throat, tied in the harvest knot, was a red ribbon.
The other seven knew that knot. They had seen it over every door in the valley, the night they burned it.

sections.heading: III. Salt and Paper
paragraphs: Lord Itagaki laughed at the first death. A drunk with a bad heart, he said, and some joker with a ribbon.

At the next harvest moon, the man who had carried the pitch died on patrol between two torchbearers who swore they had heard nothing but wind. At the one after, the man who had lit the fields died in a storehouse locked from outside. Both were light as straw. Both wore the ribbon.
Itagaki stopped laughing.

He brought the five who were left into his castle and hired priests from three temples. They pasted paper charms on every door and beam, laid salt across every threshold, and chanted sutras in shifts through the night of the harvest moon.

In the morning the fourth man was dead in the middle of them. Every charm in the room had curled and browned at the edges, like rice leaves in a drought. The salt across the doorway was unbroken, but something long had been dragged over it, back and forth, as lightly as cloth.

The fifth took vows and died at the altar of a mountain temple, monks chanting on either side. The sixth sailed to the northern coast, as far from rice as a man can get, and was found on a fish-drying rack with white hair and a ribbon at his throat. The seventh hanged himself a week before the moon. When they cut him down, there was already a ribbon beneath the rope.

Itagaki grew afraid of the wind. He had every rice field in his province cut green before the harvest moon, so that nothing ripe would be standing to whisper, and his own villages starved that winter as Hamura’s army had. It made no difference. He heard the hush in the reeds of his moat, the pines of his courtyard, the silk of his own sleeves when he turned in his sleep.
At last he sent for Jōkai, a mountain ascetic who had bound eleven ghosts. A ghost is held by its bones, so Jōkai went to Kurosawa to find them.

Inside the black stockade lay two hundred and eleven skeletons. At the gate he found the oak bar hacked two thirds through, the chain gone, and the shape of a kneeling man burned into the ground like a shadow. There were no bones in it.
He gave the two hundred and eleven their rites. Then he came back to the castle and refused his fee.
“The dead of that valley are at rest,” he told Itagaki. “The thing at the gate is not one of them. The dead want peace. That wants the harvest.”
“What harvest?” said Itagaki.
Jōkai looked at him a long time. “What did you take?” he said, and left that night.

sections.heading: IV. The Ring of Fire
paragraphs: The last soldier was their captain, who had given the order to bar the gate. He lasted until the eighth harvest moon. Then there was only Itagaki.

On the night of the ninth harvest moon, he sat in the innermost room of his keep, ringed by a hundred of his best men with swords drawn. There were lamps at every pillar and monks along every wall. The doors were nailed shut. The moat had been drained, its reeds burned, the pines felled, the courtyard raked to bare earth, so that nothing could whisper.
He had not slept a night through in nine years.
At midnight the lamps began to turn green, one at a time, from the walls inward, as if something were walking toward him.
The chanting stopped. It did not falter; it stopped mid-word, as though every monk had been hushed. Then he heard it.
Shhh.

Not in the courtyard. In the room. A hundred men stood around him and not one of them moved. Their eyes were open and their swords were raised. And along the floor between their feet came the slow scrape of iron chain over wooden boards.

It stood in front of him. Up close it smelled of wet ash and scorched rice. Its hem was black, and its hair hung over its face, and through the strands he saw green fire where its eyes should have been.
Itagaki had prepared for this. He had read the tax rolls of Kurosawa, every household, every name. He went to his knees.
“I know you,” he said. “You are Toma. The farmer at the gate. I will rebuild your village. I will give you shrines, rice, a hundred years of prayers. Toma. Toma, listen to me.”

It tilted its head at the sound, the way a dog tilts its head at a word it has almost heard before. Then it straightened. Whatever had been Toma was still kneeling in the ash at the gate. Nothing in the white robe knew that name.
It drove the sickle into the floor. Green fire went up in a ring around them both, as high as the ceiling, and closed.
Itagaki understood then. He was inside, and the way out was barred.

In the morning his men woke on their feet, swords still raised, grey-faced and white-haired, and not one of them could remember the night. In the middle of the room a ring was burned black into the floorboards, and in the middle of the ring lay the lord of the province, light as straw, with a red ribbon at his throat in the harvest knot.

sections.heading: V. Hollow Harvest
paragraphs: That should have been the end of it. The men who barred the gate were dead, Itagaki was dead, and his line soon after. The valley went back to grass.
It did not stop.
Now it walks the duelling rings, and no one has ever seen it arrive. A name goes up on the board against an empty space, and that night the lamps burn green. The fighters call it Hollow Harvest.

It does not speak, and it does not bow. It stands at the far side of the ring in the long white robe, the hem dragging through the sand, black hair over its face and red ribbons knotted through the black. The crowd goes quiet without meaning to. Then the chain begins to swing.

It fights at the full length of the chain, the sickle coming out of the dark and back to its hand. Every cut takes something. Fighters it has touched say it does not hurt so much as empty you, like grain poured from a sack, and the green fire on the blade burns brighter. It never looks any less gaunt. Pressed, it drives the sickle into the floor and soulfire bursts up in a ring around it, and the older fighters from the east will not stand inside. They know what a ring of fire means when the gate is barred.
There are more ribbons in its hair than there were doors in Kurosawa. After every bout, there is one more.

Nobody knows what it is still harvesting for. Some say it is gathering back the two hundred and twelve lives the fire took, one cut at a time, and does not know when to stop. Some say it has forgotten why, and the harvest is all that is left. Some say it is waiting for one more name on one more board.

The fighters who have faced it agree on one thing. The worst part is not the chain, or the fire, or the cold that comes after. It is the moment just before it cuts, when the arena goes still and they hear it, low and patient, like wind through ripe stalks in a valley that is not there anymore.
“Shhh…”
It is the sound a field makes just before the reaping.
